The Kalman update and the ensemble gain

The analysis step of every filter in this library is built around one matrix, the Kalman gain. It says how far to move the state for a given misfit in observation space. This chapter derives it, replaces its covariances with sample statistics, and then turns to the question that shapes the implementation: how to solve against the innovation covariance.

Three things organise it. The gain follows from asking for the best linear update, which a reader can verify by hand. The solve has two routes, a dense one and a Woodbury one, and the cheaper route depends only on the shapes. And the same innovation covariance gives the diagnostics, through innovation_statistics, so its accuracy decides what those numbers can tell you.

The best linear unbiased update¶

Let the state have the forecast mean μx∈RDx\gvect{\mu}_x \in \mathbb{R}^{D_x}μx​∈RDx​ and covariance Σx∈RDx×Dx\gmat{\Sigma}_x \in \mathbb{R}^{D_x \times D_x}Σx​∈RDx​×Dx​, and observe it with a linear H∈RDy×Dx\mat{H} \in \mathbb{R}^{D_y \times D_x}H∈RDy​×Dx​, y=Hx+ε\vect{y} = \mat{H} \vect{x} + \gvect{\varepsilon}y=Hx+ε. Seek an estimate that is linear in the residual r=y−Hμx∈RDy\vect{r} = \vect{y} - \mat{H} \gvect{\mu}_x \in \mathbb{R}^{D_y}r=y−Hμx​∈RDy​:

x^=μx+Gr,G∈RDx×Dy.\hat{\vect{x}} = \gvect{\mu}_x + \mat{G} \vect{r}, \qquad \mat{G} \in \mathbb{R}^{D_x \times D_y}.x^=μx​+Gr,G∈RDx​×Dy​.
(4.1)

It is unbiased for any G\mat{G}G, because E[r]=0\mathbb{E}[\vect{r}] = \vect{0}E[r]=0. Its error is x−x^=(I−GH)(x−μx)−Gε\vect{x} - \hat{\vect{x}} = (\mat{I} - \mat{G} \mat{H})(\vect{x} - \gvect{\mu}_x) - \mat{G} \gvect{\varepsilon}x−x^=(I−GH)(x−μx​)−Gε, and the two terms are independent, so its covariance is

Σx∣y=(I−GH)Σx(I−GH)⊤+GΣεG⊤.\gmat{\Sigma}_{x \mid y} = (\mat{I} - \mat{G} \mat{H}) \gmat{\Sigma}_x (\mat{I} - \mat{G} \mat{H})^\top + \mat{G} \gmat{\Sigma}_\varepsilon \mat{G}^\top.Σx∣y​=(I−GH)Σx​(I−GH)⊤+GΣε​G⊤.
(4.2)

Choosing G\mat{G}G to minimise the total variance tr(Σx∣y)\op{tr}(\gmat{\Sigma}_{x \mid y})tr(Σx∣y​), and setting the derivative with respect to G\mat{G}G to zero, gives −2(I−GH)ΣxH⊤+2GΣε=0-2 (\mat{I} - \mat{G} \mat{H}) \gmat{\Sigma}_x \mat{H}^\top + 2 \mat{G} \gmat{\Sigma}_\varepsilon = \mat{0}−2(I−GH)Σx​H⊤+2GΣε​=0. Collecting the G\mat{G}G terms leaves the gain Kalman, 1960:

G=ΣxyΣy−1,Σxy=ΣxH⊤,Σy=HΣxH⊤+Σε.\mat{G} = \gmat{\Sigma}_{xy} \gmat{\Sigma}_y^{-1}, \qquad \gmat{\Sigma}_{xy} = \gmat{\Sigma}_x \mat{H}^\top, \qquad \gmat{\Sigma}_y = \mat{H} \gmat{\Sigma}_x \mat{H}^\top + \gmat{\Sigma}_\varepsilon.G=Σxy​Σy−1​,Σxy​=Σx​H⊤,Σy​=HΣx​H⊤+Σε​.
(4.3)

Now substitute back into (4.2). Expanding gives (I−GH)Σx−(Σxy−GΣy)G⊤(\mat{I} - \mat{G} \mat{H}) \gmat{\Sigma}_x - (\gmat{\Sigma}_{xy} - \mat{G} \gmat{\Sigma}_y) \mat{G}^\top(I−GH)Σx​−(Σxy​−GΣy​)G⊤, and the bracket vanishes at the optimum, so

Σx∣y=(I−GH)Σx=Σx−GΣxy⊤.\gmat{\Sigma}_{x \mid y} = (\mat{I} - \mat{G} \mat{H}) \gmat{\Sigma}_x = \gmat{\Sigma}_x - \mat{G} \gmat{\Sigma}_{xy}^\top.Σx∣y​=(I−GH)Σx​=Σx​−GΣxy⊤​.
(4.4)

The short form holds only at the optimal gain, whereas (4.2) holds for any G\mat{G}G.

Nothing above assumed Gaussian errors, only their first two moments. If they are Gaussian, the same formulas are the exact posterior mean and covariance, because x\vect{x}x and y\vect{y}y are then jointly Gaussian. The gain also reads as a regression coefficient: it is the covariance of the state with the observation, divided by the variance of the observation.

The ensemble gain¶

An ensemble has no Σx\gmat{\Sigma}_xΣx​, but it has the sample statistics of chapter 3, with c=NE−1c = N_\mathcal{E} - 1c=NE​−1:

G^=Σ^xyΣ^y−1,Σ^xy=1cX~⊤H~,Σ^y=1cH~⊤H~+Σε.\hat{\mat{G}} = \hat{\gmat{\Sigma}}_{xy} \hat{\gmat{\Sigma}}_y^{-1}, \qquad \hat{\gmat{\Sigma}}_{xy} = \frac{1}{c} \tilde{\mat{X}}^\top \tilde{\mat{H}}, \qquad \hat{\gmat{\Sigma}}_y = \frac{1}{c} \tilde{\mat{H}}^\top \tilde{\mat{H}} + \gmat{\Sigma}_\varepsilon.G^=Σ^xy​Σ^y−1​,Σ^xy​=c1​X~⊤H~,Σ^y​=c1​H~⊤H~+Σε​.
(4.5)

The mean update and the covariance then have the same form as above:

xˉt∣t=xˉ+G^rˉ,Σ^x∣y=Σ^x−G^Σ^xy⊤.\bar{\vect{x}}_{t \mid t} = \bar{\vect{x}} + \hat{\mat{G}} \bar{\vect{r}}, \qquad \hat{\gmat{\Sigma}}_{x \mid y} = \hat{\gmat{\Sigma}}_x - \hat{\mat{G}} \hat{\gmat{\Sigma}}_{xy}^\top.xˉt∣t​=xˉ+G^rˉ,Σ^x∣y​=Σ^x​−G^Σ^xy⊤​.
(4.6)

For a linear hhh this is the Kalman update on the sample covariance. For a nonlinear hhh it is the statistical linearisation of chapter 3. Filters differ in how they turn this into an ensemble: chapter 5 applies G^\hat{\mat{G}}G^ to each member’s own perturbed residual, and chapter 6 transforms the anomalies without forming it.

Two routes to the solve¶

Σ^xy\hat{\gmat{\Sigma}}_{xy}Σ^xy​ is a dense Dx×DyD_x \times D_yDx​×Dy​ array, which costs O(NEDxDy)O(N_\mathcal{E} D_x D_y)O(NE​Dx​Dy​). The interesting part is the solve against Σ^y∈RDy×Dy\hat{\gmat{\Sigma}}_y \in \mathbb{R}^{D_y \times D_y}Σ^y​∈RDy​×Dy​, which is a structured matrix plus a term of rank at most ccc.

The dense route forms it and factorises it, at O(NEDy2+Dy3)O(N_\mathcal{E} D_y^2 + D_y^3)O(NE​Dy2​+Dy3​).

The Woodbury route keeps the two parts separate. Write the anomaly term with the factor Uh=H~⊤/c∈RDy×NE\mat{U}_h = \tilde{\mat{H}}^\top / \sqrt{c} \in \mathbb{R}^{D_y \times N_\mathcal{E}}Uh​=H~⊤/c​∈RDy​×NE​, so that Σ^y=Σε+UhUh⊤\hat{\gmat{\Sigma}}_y = \gmat{\Sigma}_\varepsilon + \mat{U}_h \mat{U}_h^\topΣ^y​=Σε​+Uh​Uh⊤​. The Woodbury identity Hager, 1989 then gives

Σ^y−1=Σε−1−Σε−1H~⊤(cI+H~Σε−1H~⊤)−1H~Σε−1,\hat{\gmat{\Sigma}}_y^{-1} = \gmat{\Sigma}_\varepsilon^{-1} - \gmat{\Sigma}_\varepsilon^{-1} \tilde{\mat{H}}^\top \big(c \mat{I} + \tilde{\mat{H}} \gmat{\Sigma}_\varepsilon^{-1} \tilde{\mat{H}}^\top\big)^{-1} \tilde{\mat{H}} \gmat{\Sigma}_\varepsilon^{-1},Σ^y−1​=Σε−1​−Σε−1​H~⊤(cI+H~Σε−1​H~⊤)−1H~Σε−1​,
(4.7)

which can be checked by multiplying by Σ^y\hat{\gmat{\Sigma}}_yΣ^y​. The bracket is Λw\gmat{\Lambda}_wΛw​ of chapter 6, so this route and the ETKF invert the same NE×NEN_\mathcal{E} \times N_\mathcal{E}NE​×NE​ matrix. In terms of Uh\mat{U}_hUh​ it is ccc times the capacitance I+Uh⊤Σε−1Uh\mat{I} + \mat{U}_h^\top \gmat{\Sigma}_\varepsilon^{-1} \mat{U}_hI+Uh⊤​Σε−1​Uh​, whose determinant gives the log-determinant:

log⁡∣Σ^y∣=log⁡∣Σε∣+log⁡∣I+Uh⊤Σε−1Uh∣.\log \vert \hat{\gmat{\Sigma}}_y \vert = \log \vert \gmat{\Sigma}_\varepsilon \vert + \log \big\vert \mat{I} + \mat{U}_h^\top \gmat{\Sigma}_\varepsilon^{-1} \mat{U}_h \big\vert.log∣Σ^y​∣=log∣Σε​∣+log∣∣​I+Uh⊤​Σε−1​Uh​∣∣​.
(4.8)

With Σε−1\gmat{\Sigma}_\varepsilon^{-1}Σε−1​ cheap to apply, this route costs O(NE2Dy+NE3)O(N_\mathcal{E}^2 D_y + N_\mathcal{E}^3)O(NE2​Dy​+NE3​) and never forms Σε\gmat{\Sigma}_\varepsilonΣε​. It needs Σε\gmat{\Sigma}_\varepsilonΣε​ to be positive definite.

The cheaper route depends on which matrix is smaller, and so filterax chooses by shape:

RouteDefault whenCost of the solveFactorisesNeeds
DenseNE≥DyN_\mathcal{E} \ge D_yNE​≥Dy​O(NEDy2+Dy3)O(N_\mathcal{E} D_y^2 + D_y^3)O(NE​Dy2​+Dy3​)Dy×DyD_y \times D_yDy​×Dy​Σε\gmat{\Sigma}_\varepsilonΣε​ positive semi-definite
WoodburyNE<DyN_\mathcal{E} < D_yNE​<Dy​O(NE2Dy+NE3)O(N_\mathcal{E}^2 D_y + N_\mathcal{E}^3)O(NE2​Dy​+NE3​)NE×NEN_\mathcal{E} \times N_\mathcal{E}NE​×NE​Σε\gmat{\Sigma}_\varepsilonΣε​ positive definite

A satellite swath with Dy=105D_y = 10^5Dy​=105 and NE=50N_\mathcal{E} = 50NE​=50 shows the difference: about 2.5×1082.5 \times 10^82.5×108 operations through Woodbury, against 1015 for the dense factorisation. In the opposite regime the capacitance is the larger matrix, and forming Σ^y\hat{\gmat{\Sigma}}_yΣ^y​ is what saves the work.

Implementation in filterax¶

The Layer 0 functions below build the update, and each takes the mapped ensemble or applies hhh itself.

FunctionReturnsFormula
kalman_gain(particles, obs_particles, obs_noise)dense Dx×DyD_x \times D_yDx​×Dy​ array(4.5)
cross_covariance(particles, obs_particles)dense Dx×DyD_x \times D_yDx​×Dy​ arrayΣ^xy\hat{\gmat{\Sigma}}_{xy}Σ^xy​
innovation_covariance(obs_particles, obs_noise)gaussx.LowRankUpdateΣ^y\hat{\gmat{\Sigma}}_yΣ^y​
log_likelihood(innovation, innovation_cov)scalarlog⁡N(rˉ;0,Σ^y)\log \mathcal{N}(\bar{\vect{r}}; \vect{0}, \hat{\gmat{\Sigma}}_y)logN(rˉ;0,Σ^y​)
innovation_statistics(particles, obs, obs_op, obs_noise)a dict of four results(4.9) below
localized_kalman_gain(..., rho_xy, rho_yy)dense Dx×DyD_x \times D_yDx​×Dy​ array(4.12) below

kalman_gain takes solver= to override the structural dispatch of gaussx, and dense_innovation= to force a route. The gain itself is formed as a dense array on purpose, since the analysis uses it once and DyD_yDy​ is the per-window observation count.

Algorithm¶

Program 4.1 writes the two routes out in numpy, as references for what follows.

Agreement with a dense reference¶

Program 4.2 compares kalman_gain with these references, on the default route and on both forced routes. It covers one shape on each side of the rule, plus a very small ensemble.

It prints:

NEN_\mathcal{E}NE​DyD_yDy​Default routeWoodbury by handDefaultForced denseForced Woodbury
2510dense2e-154e-164e-162e-15
2540Woodbury4e-153e-151e-153e-15
820Woodbury3e-153e-151e-153e-15

The errors are the largest absolute difference from gain_formed. Every route matches the dense reference to float64 round-off, and so does the hand-written Woodbury form (4.7).

The derivation can also be checked directly. Program 4.3 evaluates the gradient of the total variance at the sample gain, where it should vanish. It compares the two forms of the covariance there and away from the optimum. It then applies (4.6) to a real ensemble and compares it with the ETKF, which must have the same mean and covariance.

It prints 7e-16, 3e-16, 0.115 and 6e-16 6e-16. The gradient vanishes at G^\hat{\mat{G}}G^, the two forms agree there, and they differ once the gain is scaled by 1.1. The last line says that (4.6) is what the ETKF computes.

Differentiating the gain¶

Both routes are differentiable, so the gain can sit inside a training loop (chapter 14). Program 4.4 differentiates with respect to the noise variance on each route, and compares with a central difference.

It prints 3: 0.445424 0.445424 and 30: -9.795411 -9.795411, the first on the dense route and the second through Woodbury.

Innovation statistics¶

The residual and its covariance tell you whether the filter’s picture of itself is consistent with the data, and innovation_statistics returns them. Define the whitened residual rˉw∈RDy\bar{\vect{r}}_\text{w} \in \mathbb{R}^{D_y}rˉw​∈RDy​ and the log-likelihood of the forecast:

rˉw=Σ^y−1/2rˉ,log⁡p(y)=−12(Dylog⁡2π+log⁡∣Σ^y∣+rˉ⊤Σ^y−1rˉ).\bar{\vect{r}}_\text{w} = \hat{\gmat{\Sigma}}_y^{-1/2} \bar{\vect{r}}, \qquad \log p(\vect{y}) = -\frac{1}{2} \big(D_y \log 2 \pi + \log \vert \hat{\gmat{\Sigma}}_y \vert + \bar{\vect{r}}^\top \hat{\gmat{\Sigma}}_y^{-1} \bar{\vect{r}}\big).rˉw​=Σ^y−1/2​rˉ,logp(y)=−21​(Dy​log2π+log∣Σ^y​∣+rˉ⊤Σ^y−1​rˉ).
(4.9)

The function returns four things:

KeyValueHow it is computed
innovationrˉ=y−hˉ\bar{\vect{r}} = \vect{y} - \bar{\vect{h}}rˉ=y−hˉdirect
innovation_covΣ^y\hat{\gmat{\Sigma}}_yΣ^y​a gaussx.LowRankUpdate of obs_noise
normalized_innovationrˉw\bar{\vect{r}}_\text{w}rˉw​the principal root, by a contour quadrature of 30 shifted solves
log_likelihoodlog⁡p(y)\log p(\vect{y})logp(y)by QR when NE>DyN_\mathcal{E} > D_yNE​>Dy​, else through (4.7) and (4.8)

The principal root does not depend on the order of the observations, whereas a Cholesky factor would. With NE>DyN_\mathcal{E} > D_yNE​>Dy​ the shifted solves use a formed Σ^y\hat{\gmat{\Sigma}}_yΣ^y​, and otherwise they go through Woodbury.

The QR route exists because NE>DyN_\mathcal{E} > D_yNE​>Dy​ makes the capacitance the larger system, and forming Σ^y\hat{\gmat{\Sigma}}_yΣ^y​ would square its condition number. Stack the factors, S=[UhΣε1/2]⊤\mat{S} = \begin{bmatrix} \mat{U}_h & \gmat{\Sigma}_\varepsilon^{1/2} \end{bmatrix}^\topS=[Uh​​Σε1/2​​]⊤, and take the triangular factor T∈RDy×Dy\mat{T} \in \mathbb{R}^{D_y \times D_y}T∈RDy​×Dy​ of its thin QR. Then T⊤T=S⊤S=Σ^y\mat{T}^\top \mat{T} = \mat{S}^\top \mat{S} = \hat{\gmat{\Sigma}}_yT⊤T=S⊤S=Σ^y​, and

log⁡∣Σ^y∣=2∑ilog⁡∣[T]ii∣,rˉ⊤Σ^y−1rˉ=∥T−⊤rˉ∥22,\log \vert \hat{\gmat{\Sigma}}_y \vert = 2 \sum_i \log \vert [\mat{T}]_{ii} \vert, \qquad \bar{\vect{r}}^\top \hat{\gmat{\Sigma}}_y^{-1} \bar{\vect{r}} = \Vert \mat{T}^{-\top} \bar{\vect{r}} \Vert_2^2,log∣Σ^y​∣=2i∑​log∣[T]ii​∣,rˉ⊤Σ^y−1​rˉ=∥T−⊤rˉ∥22​,
(4.10)

at O(NEDy2)O(N_\mathcal{E} D_y^2)O(NE​Dy2​). Filter analyses report the same quantity, as AnalysisResult.log_likelihood.

Program 4.5 checks all four against a dense reference with a nonlinear hhh, on each side of the rule.

It prints 30 ['0e+00', '2e-16', '2e-16', '2e-16'], 4 ['0e+00', '6e-17', '2e-16', '9e-16'] and LowRankUpdate (3, 4), so every result matches the reference to round-off on both routes.

Consistency¶

If the model is right, the residual should look like a draw with the covariance Σy\gmat{\Sigma}_yΣy​, so that χ2=rˉ⊤Σ^y−1rˉ\chi^2 = \bar{\vect{r}}^\top \hat{\gmat{\Sigma}}_y^{-1} \bar{\vect{r}}χ2=rˉ⊤Σ^y−1​rˉ has mean DyD_yDy​ and ∥rˉw∥2=χ2\Vert \bar{\vect{r}}_\text{w} \Vert^2 = \chi^2∥rˉw​∥2=χ2. That is the basis of the observation-space checks of Desroziers et al. (2005). A finite ensemble shifts it, because hˉ\bar{\vect{h}}hˉ has its own sampling error and because Σ^y−1\hat{\gmat{\Sigma}}_y^{-1}Σ^y−1​ is noisy:

E[rˉrˉ⊤]=Σy+1NEHΣxH⊤.\mathbb{E}\big[\bar{\vect{r}} \bar{\vect{r}}^\top\big] = \gmat{\Sigma}_y + \frac{1}{N_\mathcal{E}} \mat{H} \gmat{\Sigma}_x \mat{H}^\top.E[rˉrˉ⊤]=Σy​+NE​1​HΣx​H⊤.
(4.11)

Program 4.6 measures the mean of χ2\chi^2χ2 on a twin experiment in which everything is correctly specified, including a truth drawn from the same density as the members.

It prints:

A value above Dy=3D_y = 3Dy​=3 at small NEN_\mathcal{E}NE​ is therefore not evidence of a bad model. Read the statistic against what the same ensemble size gives on a correct model, and see chapter 13 for how to use it in practice.

Float32 and small observation noise¶

Both routes lose accuracy when the noise is small, and they lose it differently. The dense route has only the condition number of Σ^y\hat{\gmat{\Sigma}}_yΣ^y​ to contend with. The Woodbury route inverts Σε\gmat{\Sigma}_\varepsilonΣε​ and then subtracts a nearly equal quantity, so with noise small against the ensemble term it cancels badly. Program 4.7 measures the relative error of the gain against a float64 reference, and the absolute error of the log-likelihood.

It prints:

NEN_\mathcal{E}NE​DyD_yDy​VariancesDenseWoodbury
303all 12e-071e-07
303all 10-41e-071e-03
30310-6 to 1066e-081e-02
512all 14e-073e-07
512all 10-41e-033e-03

With NE≥DyN_\mathcal{E} \ge D_yNE​≥Dy​ the default dense route holds float32 accuracy even when the variances span twelve decades, and forcing Woodbury there costs several digits. With NE<DyN_\mathcal{E} < D_yNE​<Dy​ Woodbury is the default, and a small noise variance costs digits on either route, so use float64 there. Chapter 18 collects these limits across the library.

The QR route of the log-likelihood exists for the same reason. Program 4.8 compares it with the structured route, log_likelihood on innovation_covariance, at a small noise variance.

It prints:

Noise varianceQRStructured operator
12e-072e-07
10-43e-075e-06
10-63e-072e-02

The QR route holds float32 accuracy throughout, while the structured route loses it as the noise shrinks. Filters and innovation_statistics take the QR route when NE>DyN_\mathcal{E} > D_yNE​>Dy​, so this cost falls only on a direct call to log_likelihood.

When it breaks¶

The gain carries the sampling noise of its covariances. A true correlation of zero appears in Σ^xy\hat{\gmat{\Sigma}}_{xy}Σ^xy​ at the size 1/c1 / \sqrt{c}1/c​ (chapter 2), so an observation moves state components it knows nothing about. Localization tapers those entries with a function of distance, ρ\rhoρ Gaspari & Cohn, 1999:

G^ρ=(ρxy∘Σ^xy)(ρyy∘Σ^h+Σε)−1,\hat{\mat{G}}_\rho = (\rho_{xy} \circ \hat{\gmat{\Sigma}}_{xy}) (\rho_{yy} \circ \hat{\gmat{\Sigma}}_h + \gmat{\Sigma}_\varepsilon)^{-1},G^ρ​=(ρxy​∘Σ^xy​)(ρyy​∘Σ^h​+Σε​)−1,
(4.12)

with the element-wise product ∘. The product destroys the low rank of Σ^h\hat{\gmat{\Sigma}}_hΣ^h​, so localized_kalman_gain always forms Σ^y\hat{\gmat{\Sigma}}_yΣ^y​ densely, at O(NEDxDy+DxDy2+Dy3)O(N_\mathcal{E} D_x D_y + D_x D_y^2 + D_y^3)O(NE​Dx​Dy​+Dx​Dy2​+Dy3​), where the middle term is the solve against DxD_xDx​ right-hand sides and dominates once Dy>NED_y > N_\mathcal{E}Dy​>NE​. Chapter 11 covers the trade-offs. Program 4.9 observes one component of a state whose components are independent, so the true gain is zero everywhere else.

It prints 0.498 0.498, 0.110 0.298, 0.000 and 0e+00. Without localization, components with no relation to the observation receive a gain of typical size 0.11, compared with the true value of 0.5 on the observed one. With the taper, nothing beyond its support of twice the half-width moves at all. With ρ≡1\rho \equiv 1ρ≡1 the function reduces to the plain gain.

The analysis variance is biased low. The gain is a nonlinear function of the sample covariance, and the analysis variance is concave in it. For one component with variance vvv and noise variance sss, (4.4) gives the analysis variance vs/(v+s)v s / (v + s)vs/(v+s), which is concave in vvv. Jensen’s inequality then says that an unbiased v^\hat{v}v^ gives E[v^s/(v^+s)]≤vs/(v+s)\mathbb{E}[\hat{v} s / (\hat{v} + s)] \le v s / (v + s)E[v^s/(v^+s)]≤vs/(v+s). So even with an unbiased forecast covariance, the ensemble reports too little spread after the update Leeuwen, 1999Furrer & Bengtsson, 2007Sacher & Bartello, 2008. The root of this is using the same members to estimate the gain and to be updated by it. Houtekamer & Mitchell (1998) split the ensemble in two to avoid it.

It prints:

NEN_\mathcal{E}NE​Mean of v^\hat{v}v^Mean analysis variance
51.0070.447
200.9920.485
1000.9990.497

The forecast variance is unbiased and the analysis variance is low, with the bias shrinking as the ensemble grows. It compounds over cycles, and it is one reason inflation (chapter 12) is needed.

A singular noise covariance fails through Woodbury. With NE<DyN_\mathcal{E} < D_yNE​<Dy​ and a zero variance anywhere in Σε\gmat{\Sigma}_\varepsilonΣε​, the default route returns NaN, and dense_innovation=True avoids it (chapter 3).

innovation_statistics does not scale to very many members. With NE>DyN_\mathcal{E} > D_yNE​>Dy​ it forms Σ^y\hat{\gmat{\Sigma}}_yΣ^y​ through as_matrix(), which builds an NE×NEN_\mathcal{E} \times N_\mathcal{E}NE​×NE​ matrix of weights on the way (chapter 2). At NE=200000N_\mathcal{E} = 200000NE​=200000 and Dy=3D_y = 3Dy​=3 that is a request for 160 GB in float32, which failed when we ran it. kalman_gain and filters.ETKF().analysis both completed on the same ensemble.

When to call the gain directly¶

Most users never call kalman_gain, because StochasticEnKF does it for them and the square-root filters do not form it at all. Call it when you are writing your own update, inspecting which observations move which components, or building a diagnostic such as the degrees of freedom for signal. Pass dense_innovation=False if a matrix-free solver needs the structured operator, since the default forms Σ^y\hat{\gmat{\Sigma}}_yΣ^y​ whenever NE≥DyN_\mathcal{E} \ge D_yNE​≥Dy​.

Use innovation_statistics when you want everything at once, for monitoring. For a log-likelihood alone, a filter’s AnalysisResult.log_likelihood already has it, without the 30 shifted solves of the whitened residual.
